newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-NEBIOLO ATTACKS ATLANTA FOR DESTROYING TRACK.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-NEBIOLO ATTACKS ATLANTA FOR DESTROYING TRACK.

text.p: World athletics chief Primo Nebiolo attacked on Friday the organisers of last year's Atlanta Olympics for leaving no trace of the stage where sporting history was made.

Unlike other former Olympic cities, which still boast magnificent track and field arenas, Atlanta tore up the track where American Michael Johnson completed an historic 200 and 400 metres double and turned the arena into a baseball stadium.

"At the end we had the greatest competition there (of the Games) and now it does not have a track," the president of the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) said after a meeting with the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

Outside North America, most of the former Olympic stadia around the world have become major momuments, still stage athletics events and carry the name of the Olympics. Some have become tourist attractions.

The Munich stadium, which staged the 1972 Games, for example, is the home of two leading German soccer clubs and is largely used for football. But the "Olympiastadion" still has a track and hosts international athletics competitions.
The Atlanta arena is now simply named "Turner Field" after the U.S. media magnate Ted Turner who owns the Atlanta Braves who play there.

"Ted Turner is a great friend of mine but unfortunately he was not close to us during the Olympic Games," Nebiolo said after the IAAF council met IOC president Juan Antonio Samaranch and leading Olympic officials on the eve of the world championships.
Nebiolo continued his campaign to get athletics more money from the Games.
The IAAF chief said he wanted more serious talks with the IOC about cash after Samaranch has stood for re-election in September when the IOC will also decide which city will host the 2004 Games.

"At a world championships the revenue is $100 million and we get $8 million from the Olympics Games," Nebiolo said. "When the discussion for the bidding cities is behind us then it would be a good moment to speak about our problems."

The money made by the Olympics is huge. The IOC recently signed a television deal with the American network NBC worth more than $2 billion. The contract which the IOC has with its leading sponsors is worth around $400 million over four years.
